name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
description: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS) is a large multilingual corpus suitable for speech research. The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consists of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages (German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish). The dataset also includes Language Models (LM) and baseline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models for all languages.
creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert (Facebook AI Research)
inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert. MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. arXiv:2012.03411v2 [eess.AS], December 2020.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox. Audio data was downloaded using data preparation tools from the LibriLight open source library. All audio data is downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Audio files were segmented into 10-20 second segments using trained acoustic models. Pseudo labels were generated via beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model. Text sources for audiobooks were downloaded from multiple domains including gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, and hathitrust.org. For non-English languages, manual approaches were also used to extract text from browsers, PDFs, and EPUBs. Transcript retrieval was performed by matching pseudo labels to source text using TF-IDF similarity and Smith-Waterman alignment.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping, Web API, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For some audiobooks, text sources were unavailable due to invalid links or redirected pages. For example, all text sources from the spiegel.de domain (accounting for 1/3 of German audio data) were redirected to invalid pages. Manual searches were conducted to find alternate sources. The training data is lower than the raw LibriVox data because: 1) text sources for some audiobooks were not downloaded, 2) candidate labels were filtered during transcript retrieval, or 3) data was filtered while creating valid/test splits.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: LibriVox audiobooks (read speech) and corresponding book texts from Project Gutenberg, archive.org, ccel.org, hathitrust.org, and other online sources. LibriVox and Project Gutenberg data are released in the public domain.
rai:dataImputationProtocol: Numbers in the matched text were replaced with the corresponding aligned words from the pseudo label to handle ambiguous number pronunciations and page numbers not read by speakers.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Audio was segmented into 10-20 second segments by finding the longest silence duration within the 10-20 second range and splitting at the midpoint of the silence chunk. If no silence frames were found, the audio was split at the 20-second mark. Heuristics were applied to handle hyphens and apostrophes in transcripts. Candidate transcripts with WER greater than 40% between the candidate transcript and pseudo label were filtered out. Books with corrupted metadata, multiple speakers, or duplicate versions were removed. Gender labels were assigned to speakers using an SVM classifier.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text normalization included NFKC normalization, removal of unwanted characters (punctuations, subscript/superscripts, emojis, escape symbols), removal of end-of-line hyphens, and filtering of characters outside the valid unicode range for each language's orthography. For language models, books were filtered to avoid overlap with development and test sets by removing books with edit distance less than 2 from dev/test book titles and books sharing more than 1% of 5-grams with dev/test sets. Dataset splits were created ensuring no speaker overlap between train/dev/test, gender balance in dev/test, and chapter exclusivity per partition.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Transcripts for development and test sets were human-verified. Human transcribers listened to audio files while reading the generated transcript and were asked to correct only 'clear and obvious' errors to avoid introducing bias. The transcript retrieval process used TF-IDF similarity on bigrams to find matching documents, followed by Smith-Waterman alignment with a matching score of 2 and substitution/insertion/deletion score of -1.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: WER between generated transcripts (GT) and human-rated transcripts (HRT) was measured for dev and test sets across all languages. WER ranged from 1.93% (Spanish dev) to 12.64% (Portuguese dev). Examples of corrections included diacritic corrections, missing words, and missing apostrophes.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Acoustic models using Time-Depth Separable (TDS) Convolutions with Auto-Segmentation Criterion (ASG) loss for audio segmentation; wav2letter@anywhere framework for streaming inference; beam-search decoding with 4-gram language model for pseudo label generation; SVM with RBF kernel for gender classification; KenLM toolkit for 3-gram and 5-gram language model training; wav2letter++ framework for baseline ASR models; pdftotext for extracting text from PDF/EPUB books.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is freely available at http://www.openslr.org. Pretrained models and recipes are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/wav2letter. No explicit versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker gender is labeled for all speakers using an SVM gender classifier. Speaker identity information is included (speaker IDs). Audio data used for training acoustic models used in segmentation was completely de-identified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to promote open research in large-scale ASR and multilingual ASR. It may also be used for Text-to-Speech (TTS) research. The authors believe such a large transcribed dataset will open new avenues in ASR and TTS research.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is derived from read audiobooks (read speech), which may not generalize to conversational or spontaneous speech. English is heavily dominant with 44.5K hours compared to approximately 6K hours total for all other languages. Speaker gender balance is enforced in dev and test sets but not necessarily in training sets. The gender classifier used has accuracy of 95-96% and may introduce some labeling errors.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset consists only of read speech from audiobooks, limiting generalizability to other speech domains. Polish has a high OOV rate of 13.39% in the language model, negatively impacting LM-based decoding. Some languages have significantly fewer hours than others (e.g., Polish with ~103 hours vs. English with ~44K hours). The MLS development and test sets for English are designed to be harder than LibriSpeech dev-/test-other partitions.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems; multilingual ASR research; low-resource ASR benchmarking (with provided 10-hour, 1-hour, and 10-minute limited supervision sets); Text-to-Speech (TTS) research; language model training and evaluation.
